title: The Making of Roger Scruton
author: Dan Hitchens
summary: Hitchens, senior editor at First Things, sets out to answer a question Scruton's old schoolfriends and girlfriends keep asking: how did a kind, apolitical, red-haired grammar-school boy become Britain's most hated conservative thinker? His answer is really an argument about formation. Borrowing Richard Foreman's contrast between the cathedral-like educated personality and the modern pancake person spread wide and thin, Hitchens treats Scruton as the last convincing specimen of the first type and asks how such people were once made. The answer turns out to have almost nothing to do with the official curriculum. It was the Royal Grammar School High Wycombe as a social world rather than a syllabus: a chemistry master who knew German Romanticism, a teacher who invited boys round to discuss Beethoven quartets and Durkheim, a sixth-form paper-reading society modeled on Leavis, a friend who pressed Spengler and Erich Heller into his hands, a public library and mail-order LPs. Hitchens shows Scruton absorbing from Eliot and Leavis the principle that would organize his life, that you either learn to inherit the tradition properly or you become disinherited, and then reading the Paris barricades of 1968 through that inheritance. The piece is valuable to an education archive precisely because it reconstructs, in granular detail, the off-curriculum conditions under which a dense cultural inheritance actually gets transmitted to a poor boy who had almost no books at home.
points: Hitchens frames the essay around Richard Foreman's distinction between the cathedral-like personality carrying a personal version of the whole Western heritage and the pancake people who replace inner repertory with networked access.

Scruton credited the Royal Grammar School High Wycombe with teaching him more in six years than any other period of his life, yet Hitchens shows that most of that education happened off the curriculum.

The transmission mechanism was social and informal: teachers talking out of hours, the sect-like sixth-form 13 Society reading papers on Nietzsche and Four Quartets, and friends who handed each other Spengler and Heller.
Leavis and Eliot supplied the organizing conviction Hitchens treats as Scruton's life principle, that an inheritance must be properly learned or it is simply lost.

Hitchens argues Scruton's conservatism grew less from political knowledge than from a long apprenticeship in rebellion against his father, his headmaster, and upper-class Cambridge, redirected in 1968 to defend what he loved.
quotes: If anyone in the twenty-first century exemplified the “cathedral-like” personality, a one-man version of Western civilization in its depth and breadth, it was Roger Scruton. And it is worth asking, in the age of us pancake people, how those cathedral-like personalities were once formed.

In 1954, at the age of ten, Scruton started at the Royal Grammar School High Wycombe (RGS), a leading example of the postwar schools that provided a first-rate education to children from poor and middling backgrounds.

Scruton stayed long enough to win a scholarship to Jesus College, Cambridge, but he left without completing his final year. Nevertheless, he was forever grateful for the formation he received at RGS. He learned more in his six years there, he once wrote, than in any other period of his life.

The young Scruton had “a greed for knowledge,” recalls his old schoolmate Peter Findlay. “He was interested in absolutely everything.” Findlay himself liked classical music, but then his dad had been forcing it down his throat from a young age, so blues and jazz were far more exciting. For Scruton, whose childhood home contained few books and little music, high culture became a consuming fascination.

Then there were the teachers who, out of hours, would introduce the boys to a wider culture—like Mr. Pelmore, the chemistry master who knew all about German Romanticism, and Mr. Chapman, who invited the boys round to hear his stories of imperial service in Africa and discuss Beethoven’s quartets and Durkheim’s sociology.

Both those principles could also be found in the literary criticism of F. R. Leavis, then a major presence in British intellectual life, whose study of English poetry, Revaluation, gave Scruton, as he would recall, “a tremendous belief in English culture and literature. I never thought there was an alternative to what we had inherited. You either learn to inherit it properly or you become disinherited.

He had little political knowledge. What he had—from his battles with his father and his headmaster, from his experiences as a grammar-school boy at Cambridge—was a long training in rebellion and its ironies.
In later years, he described how he and his Cambridge contemporaries entered the “cathedral” of high culture, a precious shared experience.
